text: Ceilingviz is projected onto a ceiling; user wants a calm, sleepy mood with soft colors, one single visualization, no mode switching. Explicitly rejected (user-confirmed YAGNI): settings UI, audio reactivity, constellation lines/labels, planets/moon, precession correction (~0.3deg error, invisible at projector scale), dedup of binary star components (rendering both approximates true combined brightness). Default location is Thessaloniki, overridable via ?lat=&lon=. Possible future intent: planets/moon could be added later if the user asks.

The user judged the original aurora (thick blurred wavy horizontal bands) as fake and asked for 'a 3D vertical sash of light', referencing a horizon-view aurora photograph. Rejected alternative: rendering the aurora as a radial corona with rays converging on the zenith. That would be physically consistent with the star layer, which uses a zenith-centred projection, so someone will eventually notice the mismatch and try to 'fix' it. The user chose screen-space vertical curtains anyway: a corona reads as a starburst and is not calm, and the ceiling has no true 'up' so the inconsistency is invisible in use. Do not convert the aurora to radial rays without asking.

The current look took eight rounds of visual iteration against headless Chrome captures. Empirically, these are what made it read as fake, in rough order of how strongly the eye catches them: left-right mirror symmetry between curtains; regular filament spacing and equal filament widths, which reads as an audio equaliser; hard vertical edges on rays, which read as light leaks; neon saturation and brightness, which kills the calm mood; a smooth dark lower border, which reads as a mountain ridge; and uniform filament brightness with no bright cores. Anyone re-tuning the constants should check captures against that list, because several of these were reintroduced accidentally while fixing others.

Note for future visual work here: --virtual-time-budget does not advance the animation loop, so screenshots taken that way are all the same frame and silently hide motion bugs. Drive a real Chrome session over CDP and capture seconds apart instead.

Star flicker strength was a deliberate undershoot of reality. The user was offered a stronger, more realistic option (about +/-35% RMS near the horizon, top rate about 4 Hz) and chose the gentle version instead (+/-18% near the horizon, +/-4% at the zenith, top rate 1.5 Hz). Reason: this is projected on a ceiling as a sleep aid, so calm beats accuracy. Do not "fix" the flicker by making it faster or deeper without asking.

Also rejected, user-confirmed: colour shift during twinkle. Real stars shift hue when they scintillate, but that would add warmth to a deliberately cold white palette. Rejected too: per-star size or radius modulation, and any settings UI for tuning the effect.

The aurora used to read as separate vertical pillars because each ray's colour gradient was anchored to that ray's own length, so no two rays were bright at the same altitude. The fix anchors the bright stops to a shared absolute altitude around baseY. When the user asked to connect the towers, they were offered two options and chose this one. Rejected alternative: a full-height diffuse veil pass filling the gaps at every height. It was rejected before implementation because it flattens the depth, washes out the stars behind the aurora, and raises the total light on the ceiling, which fights the calm mood. Do not add a fog/veil pass without asking.

Adds to the anti-fake list in rztcvk: the 'mountain ridge' tell has two separate causes, and fixing only one leaves it visible. (1) A soft, long fade at the bottom of the curtain. A real aurora's emission stops abruptly near 100 km, so the lower border must be a bright plateau with a short cutoff below it; a dim gradual bottom reads as a hazy hillside. (2) The two curtains' base lines forming a dome. They used to run 0.80->0.61 and 0.57->0.76, near mirror images with a 0.19 swing each, so together they arced up in the middle and the black below read as a hill silhouette. Both were hit in sequence during this change: fixing the border softness alone made the dome more obvious, not less.

Process note for visual work here: the implementing agent's model could not read images, so it optimised pixel statistics that all looked correct while the render clearly showed a ridge and, in an earlier round, hollowed-out rays. Numeric metrics did not catch either. Someone who can see the frames must do the acceptance pass.
